title: Thieves charged in royal residence burglary scaled drainpipe, stole cufflinks and a clock, police allege

image.caption: A police officer is shown Monday after a burglary was reported at Anmer Hall, a property on the Sandringham estate that belongs to the Prince and Princess of Wales. (Martin Pope/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·Updated

A British court heard cufflinks and a clock were stolen after a break-in at the Royal Family's Sandringham Estate on Monday. The two men, charged with burglary and trespassing on a protected site, appeared in court Wednesday.
2 men appeared in London court Wednesday, 1 remains at large
· Anna Cunningham
· Posted: Nov 25, 2026 5:53 AM EST | Last Updated: 2 minutes ago

When it comes to matters of royal security, nothing is taken lightly in the U.K. Responsibility falls to a specialist branch of the Metropolitan Police Service, and guaranteeing the safety and protection of senior, working royals is constantly under review.

So when police in Norfolk, a rural county in eastern England, were alerted Monday evening to suspicious activity on the King’s Sandringham estate, the response was rapid and widespread. A helicopter reportedly was in the air for some three hours. Dogs and a drone searched the extensive grounds under cover of darkness.

The response was a far cry from what the average Briton might get — a visit from some police officers, sometimes several hours after a break-in, and a reference number to follow up with later. But these are the royals.

Two men were arrested and charged on Wednesday with burglary of a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site — in this case, Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house gifted by the late Queen Elizabeth to her grandson Prince William, now next in line to the throne, and his wife, Princess Catherine, when they married in 2011.

Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, make an appearance at an event in Mumbai on Nov. 17. The couple are now back in the U.K., but were not at their country residence during Monday's break-in. (Rafiq Maqbool/The Associated Press)
Police confirmed the royal couple were not at the property at the time. Anmer Hall is not a permanent residence, but they are known to use it on weekends and holidays.
3rd suspect at large

The accused appeared in court Wednesday in Norwich. Both spoke through an Albanian interpreter, identifying themselves as 34-year-old Mirgen Doku and Arilen Ndoci, 32. Prosecutors revealed that another suspect remains at large.

The court heard details alleging the men stole six pairs of cufflinks — one set was described as "the Duke of Edinburgh cufflinks" — and a clock after climbing up a drainpipe into the royal property and forcing entry into a dressing room.

The Magistrates' Court was told motion sensors were triggered outside Anmer Hall at around 6 p.m. local time Monday. A game and conservation manager, who was on duty in the estate carrying out what was described as a "hare patrol" reportedly saw two men jump through a hedgerow and into the woods.
The court heard that, along with the heat-seeking equipment on the police helicopter, the estate worker helped in the search using a thermal spotter.
A police forensics van sits near Anmer Hall on Tuesday. The 10-bedroom home is often used as a country retreat for the family. (Martin Pope/Getty Images)
Prosecutors said the two men were not wearing shoes when they were detained.
Neither man entered any pleas during his court appearance, and both were remanded in custody to reappear Monday.

Anmer Hall is where the Princess of Wales spent time after her cancer diagnosis and features in a video marking the end of her chemotherapy. The location has also been a backdrop for many photos of William and Catherine with their children Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.
Property open to public part of year

The property is a short drive from Sandringham House, King Charles and Queen Camilla’s country retreat. For six months of the year the house and gardens are open to the public for visits. Traditionally, it’s where the Royal Family spends Christmas and New Year's Eve.
The sprawling estate is also home to the King’s brother and former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who moved to Marsh Farm in Sandringham in April.

Security breaches at royal properties remain rare, but they have happened. In 2021, on Christmas Day, a man was found in Windsor Castle grounds armed with a crossbow. He was later sentenced to nine years in prison.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince, leaves a police station in Aylsham, U.K., on Feb. 19. Mountbatten-Windsor has lived in Marsh Farm, on Sandringham estate, since April. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

The most serious security lapse happened in 1982, when Queen Elizabeth, asleep in her bedroom in Buckingham Palace, woke to find an intruder in her room. She spoke with him for about ten minutes before the alarm was raised.
Kensington Palace — William and Catherine's official residence — has previously said they do not comment on security matters.
